She turns to Christianity to relieve the pain in her heart, but when even this is not permitted, she wages a war against God.

Over a series of clandestine meetings, the two begin an improbable relationship that defies the judgment and cruelty of the world around them.

Join us in the microcinema for Alex Prager’s stylish dystopian satire *DreamQuil *– an unsettling science fiction mystery starring Elizabeth Banks, John C. Reilly, and Juliette Lewis. Set in the not so distant future when poor air quality leads to people living mostly virtual lives. Carol (Banks) is a dissatisfied career mother, struggling to find connection within her marriage to Gary (Reilly) and to her child. With the day to day familiarity of their home and lives feeling increasingly claustrophobic, and worried she could be heading towards divorce, Carol leaps at the chance to get her life back on track by signing up for DreamQuil, an avant-garde digital wellness retreat. When Carol returns home however, she discovers her family has been living with “Carol Two”, a home robot the corporation sent designed to help in her absence, and things take a mysterious and sinister turn.
An anthology of various tales told in various styles with robots being the one common element among them.

BURNING is the searing examination of an alienated young man, Jongsu (Ah-in Yoo), a frustrated introvert whose already difficult life is complicated by the appearance of two people in his orbit: first, Haemi (newcomer Jong-seo Jun), a spirited woman who offers the romantic possibility, and then, Ben (Steven Yeun), a wealthy and sophisticated young man she returns from a trip with. However, when Jongsu learns of Ben’s mysterious hobby and Haemi suddenly disappears, his confusion and obsessions begin to mount, culminating in a stunning finale.

One of maestro Pedro Almodóvar’s most-complicated and lauded masterpieces, this exquisitely shot meditation on loyalty and obsession earned Almodóvar the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay along with the Golden Globe and BAFTA Awards for best Foreign Language Film. With a breathtaking and controversial mix of movement and stillness, murky morality, and outrageously envelope-pushing imagery and subject matter- Almodóvar creates a world with sympathy for monsters, oversized genitalia, and Pina Bausch performances no one should miss on the big screen. Two men (Benigno and Marco) almost meet while watching a dance performance (of German icon Pina Bausch no less), but their lives are irrevocably entwined by fate. They meet later at a private clinic where Benigno is the caregiver for Alicia, a beautiful dance student who lies in a coma. Marco is there to visit his girlfriend, Lydia, a famous matador, also rendered motionless. As the men wage vigil over the women they love, the story unfolds in flashback and flash-forward as the lives of the four are further entwined and their relationships move toward a shocking conclusion.

Martin Sellers) meets the eccentric Gretta (the incredible Meridith Haze in her only known role) working at the carnival, stuffs a few hundred dollar bills down her shirt and takes her home. After seeing one of her films in his dorm, college student Glenn Marshall (Rick Barnes) becomes infatuated with the actress, and follows the clues from the adult store where the film was rented, to the production company that produced the picture, eventually finding himself face to face with Gretta, who is playing the piano pantsless at the shady "Club Manhattan". Glenn is sucked into a dangerous triad, and what follows becomes more incredulous from one moment to the next, including getting caught up in the titular "Death Wish Club".

Gender swapping, seances, giant bug POV shots, demolition balls, electric chairs, karate, and so much more await you in DEATH WISH CLUB.

Every space hosts the accumulation of time and is thus a repository of memory, one that is active and dynamic.

Jean Khalil Chamoun’s *Women Beyond Borders* (2004) and Theo Panagopoulos’ *The Flowers Stand Silently, Witnessin*g (2024) were made two decades apart, but together they foster an ongoing conversation at the intersection of identity, memory and place across Lebanon and Palestine.

Though distinct in form, the films consider the relationship between people’s lived environments and their individual and collective identities. The films navigate through spaces both historically and presently marked by displacement, violence and resilience. Both offer meditations and testimonies on how these spaces can inhabit a people’s memories, linger into their present realities and influence their futures.

Rather than attempting to unearth a singular tradition, this program amplifies an ongoing cinematic conversation across Lebanon and Palestine that is rooted in intertwined histories of occupation and resistance. This conversation is an urgent one to hold today in light of the ongoing aggression against southern Lebanon and historic Palestine that continues to target complete ecosystems. This systematic surge of destruction and harm affects far beyond the physical; it seeks to fracture memory, sever a people’s sense of being and belonging, and jeopardize social relations that places sustain. The moving image as a tool presents an opportunity to forge an alternative place of memory work, one capable of preserving spatial memory, making visible the forms of erasure, and imagining continuities that exceed the violence of occupation and its imposed restriction on bodies and space.

*Programmed by UCLA Comparative Literature Ph.D. student Aciah Abdulsater and Archive Research and Public Access Coordinator Nicole Ucedo. Notes and concept by Aciah Abdulsater.*

Hearing those colors unfold through the Metropole Orkest has been profoundly moving.”

At the heart of CIANI/ORKEST lies Ciani’s lifelong commitment to quadraphonic sound. From her early Buchla performances in the late 1960s to her 2018 release LIVE Quadraphonic, Ciani has treated space as a primary compositional parameter. Working alongside immersive producer KamranV, Ciani continues to explore immersive sound as both artistic and human gesture. Kamran’s decades of work in spatial formats, converge here in service of a singular goal: to let sound behave as it does in the physical world.

*Archive Talks* pairs leading historians and scholars with screenings of the moving image media that is the focus of their writing and research. Each program will begin with a special talk by the invited scholar that will introduce audiences to new insights, interpretations and contexts for the films and media being screened.

The Archive first worked with archivist and scholar Laura Horak in 2022 when we presented a series of films unearthed by Horak and her collaborators, Maggie Hennefeld and Elif Rongen-Kaynakçi. Their archival project *Cinema’s First Nasty Women *celebrated the work of silent comedians who brought an anarchic brand of gender non-conformity to slapstick. Alongside that work, Horak is also the director of the Transgender Media Lab at Carleton University, which created the [Transgender Media Portal](https://www.transgendermediaportal.org/), a database of trans creators, including links to where their work can be seen. Suffice it to say, increasing the visibility and access to the media she studies is an essential element of Horak’s ongoing research project. With her latest book, *Trans Cinema: Making Communities, Identities, and Worlds*, Horak dives deep into the history, practice and aesthetics of trans artists in the United States and Canada in the 21st century while positioning them within the larger history of trans media production and representation. The Archive is pleased to welcome Horak back to the Billy Wilder Theater for a brief talk about her work followed by a selection of works by trans artists and an on-stage conversation, with more special guests to be announced soon!

The legendary Suzanne Ciani joins the internationally acclaimed Metropole Orkest, conducted by Simon Dobson, for the release of [CIANI/ORKEST](http://akprecordings.com/cianiorkest), a landmark live album composed entirely of new work, created specifically for this unprecedented collaboration. Under the direction of the Metropole Orkest, renowned for its genre-defying collaborations with artists from jazz to contemporary classical – strings shimmer, brass swells and woodwinds echo the organic, fluid qualities that have always defined Ciani’s sound. “This project feels like a homecoming,” says Ciani. “The Buchla was always orchestral to me, an instrument capable of infinite color. Hearing those colors unfold through the Metropole Orkest has been profoundly moving.”

At the heart of CIANI/ORKEST lies Ciani’s lifelong commitment to quadraphonic sound. From her early Buchla performances in the late 1960s to her 2018 release LIVE Quadraphonic, Ciani has treated space as a primary compositional parameter. Working alongside immersive producer KamranV, Ciani continues to explore immersive sound as both artistic and human gesture. Kamran’s decades of work in spatial formats, converge here in service of a singular goal: to let sound behave as it does in the physical world.

The playboy and thief Gaston (Herbert Marshall) meets the expert pickpocket Lily (Miriam Hopkins) on the Riviera, and they, of course, fall in love. In Paris, Gaston gets a job as the personal secretary to a wealthy heiress to a perfume company, Mariette (Kay Francis), hiring Lily as the maid, so they can rob her blind. Unfortunately, while cleaning up the corruption on her company’s board, he also falls in love with her. No director was better at exposing the false morality of the bourgeoisie when pursuing sexual desire. Here, Ernst Lubitsch sets up a faux marriage, then turns the relationship into a ménage à trois, which he provocatively suggests may be the best way to keep a sexual relationship interesting and stable. Lubitsch’s direction of actors is almost Pirandellian, with the actors speaking their emotional lines in a virtual monotone, thus creating parodies of romantic love.

On display in this luscious pre-Code comedic romance is the creative genius of Travis Banton, one of Hollywood’s most important costume designers, whose collaborators included Lubitsch, Marlene Dietrich and Josef von Sternberg. A conversation on Banton’s influence and evocative style, with author Howard Gutner and Professor Deborah Nadoolman Landis, will precede the screening.

Premiering on NBC on October 17, 1966, *Hollywood Squares* became one of the most popular game shows in television history, with over 4,000 episodes of the original network incarnation produced through 1981. The longevity of the simple tic-tac-toe game was driven in large part by the show’s charismatic, quick-witted host, Peter Marshall. A talented actor and nightclub comedian, Marshall breezily tackled the daunting task of corralling the series’ boisterous, rotating stable of nine celebrities, setting up punchlines and volleying retorts with equal aplomb. 

While high-wattage superstars such as Vincent Price and Sammy Davis Jr. often guested, the literal center of *Hollywood Squares’ *towering, neon-lit set featured an icon like no other — actor and comedian Paul Lynde. Beloved by audiences of all stripes, Lynde routinely brought down the house with bawdy ad-libs and double entendres — delivered impeccably with a knowing wink. Painfully closeted in his personal life to protect his showbiz career, Lynde turned conventional wisdom of the day upside down, boldly introducing the masses to an undeniably empowered, queer-coded persona previously unseen on television. 

Join us as we celebrate the 60th anniversary of the premiere of *Hollywood Squares* and the birth centennials of Peter Marshall and Paul Lynde. Two preserved episodes will be screened, complete with original commercials, as well as an extended clip reel showcasing a galaxy of guest stars, risque retorts and the genius of Paul Lynde.

Hollywood Entertainment invites you to experience a rare 35mm screening of Richard Kwietniowski’s Owning Mahowny on “Brian Molony Day” – the unofficial holiday whose namesake inspired the film’s events.

In one of his most unforgettable yet under-seen performances, Philip Seymour Hoffman immerses you in the double life of Dan Mahowny, a bank employee stealing money from wealthy client accounts to gamble with in Atlantic City and Las Vegas. Casino manager Victor Foss (John Hurt) notices his high rolling and goes out of his way to enable Mahowny’s addiction, flying him and his stolen cash directly to the casinos. Dan’s compulsions cause turmoil with his girlfriend (played by Minnie Driver) and bookie (Maury Chaykin).

The real story: Brian Molony; a CIBC manager who gambled over $10 million (over $34 million today) in stolen funds via mostly sports betting and at Caesars Palace Atlantic City. Because Caesars violated reporting regulations, the state of New Jersey ordered the casino be shut down for a full day. Casino employees deemed that day (November 30, 1985) “Brian Molony Day.”

When Gary Stephen Ross, the author of *Stung: The Incredible Obsession of Brian Molony*, was asked if Hoffman’s portrayal was anything like the real Brian Molony, Ross said, “Philip somehow managed to assimilate the psychic essence of Molony – a yawning emptiness that nothing except gambling was able to fill.”

“Mr. Mahowny would like barbecue ribs- no sauce, and a coke.”

Join Vidiots and the Cinema Eye Honors in celebrating the tremendous legacy of filmmaker Shirley Clarke with a screening of her groundbreaking documentary *Portrait of Jason!*

On December 2, 1966, director Shirley Clarke and a miniscule film crew gathered in her apartment at the Hotel Chelsea. Bestowed for twelve hours with the one-and-only Jason Holliday, Clarke confronted the iconic performer about his good times and bad behavior as a gay hustler, on-and-off houseboy and aspiring cabaret performer. As the cameras rolled and Holliday spun tales, sang songs and donned costumes through the night, a mesmerizing portrait formed of a remarkable man. Ingmar Bergman called it “the most extraordinary film I’ve seen in my life,” but audiences may know it better as PORTRAIT OF JASON, a funny, stinging and painful meditation on pride and prejudice through the eyes of a legendary figure.

At the 2026 [Cinema Eye Honors](https://cinemaeyehonors.com/about/), Shirley Clarke’s *Portrait of Jason *was recognized with the Legacy Award, which recognizes films that embodies the Cinema Eye mission statement of recognizing and honoring exemplary craft and innovation in nonfiction film as well as being a film that has inspired a new generation of filmmakers to create art in the nonfiction realm.

Cinema Eye was founded in 2007 on three ideals: creating events to support and build community amongst those who make documentary films; recognizing the entire creative team of craftspersons that create these films; and recognizing excellence, innovation and boldness in the artistry of nonfiction filmmaking.

Cinema Eye was the first and remains the only international nonfiction award to recognize the whole creative team, presenting annual craft awards in directing, editing, producing, cinematography, original score, visual design and sound design. Cinema Eye presents and produces the annual Cinema Eye Week and Honors Awards Ceremony.

The Cinema Eye Honors recognize feature and short-length films and series with an emphasis on nonfiction work that is designed for public distribution, whether primarily theatrical, festival, broadcast or streaming. Cinema Eye seeks to encourage audiences to engage with nonfiction work that crosses all genres, whether observational, journalistic, activist, essayistic, light-hearted or provocative as well as those exciting works that blur the lines between nonfiction and fiction. Since its founding, Cinema Eye has sought to change the conversation that film critics, festivals and awards bodies have surrounding documentary film, shifting the emphasis from importance of topic to artistic craft.

Cinema Eye is led by a core team of filmmakers and programmers who are committed to the organization’s mission.

The great American filmmaker William Greaves, who in his illustrious career of more than 50 years documented the civil rights movement and historical figures like Muhammad Ali, Paul Robeson, Ida B. Wells, and Raphe Bunche, who executive produced the groundbreaking PBS news program *Black Journal*, and who wrote and directed the radically experimental fiction hybrid *Symbiopsychotaxiplasm*, had one last trick up his sleeve before his death in 2014: He left behind an extraordinary archive of unedited footage from a cocktail party he staged and hosted in 1972 at the home of Duke Ellington, an astonishingly vital and poignant gathering of luminaries from the Harlem Renaissance, many of whom had not seen each other for nearly a half century. Among those assembled were the artists Aaron Douglas and Romare Bearden, the composers Eubie Blake and Noble Sissle, the photographer James Van Der Zee, the poet Arna Bontemps, and the actor Leigh Whipper. Now, some 50 years later, Greaves’ son David, one of three cameramen filming that day, has shaped this never-before-seen material into the beautiful and indelible *Once Upon a Time in Harlem*, carrying on the work of Greaves’ wife and longtime partner Louise Archambault Greaves and collaborating with Greaves’ granddaughter Liani and Anne de Mare as producers.

In a trailblazing entertainment industry career spanning over half a century, producer-director Stan Lathan continues to leave an indelible creative mark. His groundbreaking work in television began with directing the PBS public affairs and documentary series *Say Brother* and *Black Journal*, which were produced to give voice to Black communities following the assassination of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Later summoned by Redd Foxx to work on *Sanford and Son* as one of the few Black directors in primetime television, Lathan went on to helm episodes for a wide range of hit series, from *Hill Street Blues* to *Roc*. A formidable talent, he also directed numerous pilots that launched highly successful series, including *Amen* and *Moesha*.

In a career of milestones, following his theatrical feature *Beat Street* (1984), Lathan partnered with Russell Simmons to create *Def Comedy Jam* and *Def Poetry Jam* for HBO, the latter garnering the duo a Peabody Award. Among multiple Emmy, Grammy and Tony Awards and too many other major awards to mention, Lathan was recognized with a CINE Golden Eagle and an American Film Festival Blue Ribbon for directing the *American Playhouse* telefilm *Go Tell It on the Mountain* (1985). In perhaps the highest accolade possible, cultural titan James Baldwin publicly pronounced his love of the TV adaptation of his seminal work.

Join us as we celebrate Stan Lathan with a screening of *Go Tell It on the Mountain*, introduced by NYU Associate Professor Josslyn Luckett.

*Programmed and notes written by John H. Mitchell Television Curator Mark Quigley.*

Adapted from James Baldwin’s semi-autobiographical novel, this acclaimed television production won the approval of the author himself, with the literary and cultural giant telling the *New York Times* that he was “very, very happy about [the film] ... it did not betray the book.” Through flashbacks, award-winning director Stan Lathan powerfully interweaves painful family histories that inform the life of sensitive, burgeoning author John Grimes (James Bond III). Against the forces of religion, racism and poverty during the Great Depression, the 14-year-old Grimes begins a path of profound self-discovery and possibilities, impeded by his emotionally abusive, preacher step-father (Paul Winfield).

Hell Houses are a distinctly American phenomenon which began in 1990 just outside of Dallas, Texas at the Trinity Assembly of God Church. The original Hell House was conceived as a modern-day fire-and-brimstone sermon. venues.bio: The legendary Santa Monica video store, reborn in 2023 as a nonprofit in Eagle Rock's 1929 Eagle Theatre — 271 seats, a bar, and 60,000 tapes.
venues.name: Vidiots

venues.bio: A 1923 single-screen theater on the Los Feliz/East Hollywood line, Spanish outside and Egyptian inside, owned by Quentin Tarantino since 2021.
venues.name: Vista Theatre

venues.bio: A VHS shop and microcinema in an Echo Park alley, open since 2022, screening rare tapes and cult finds Wednesday through Sunday.
venues.name: WHAMMY!

venues.bio: Sid Grauman's 1922 Hollywood movie palace, the first for a studio premiere, restored and run by American Cinematheque.
venues.name: Egyptian Theatre

venues.bio: A 1931 single-screen theater in Westwood Village — formerly the Fox Westwood, then Mann and Regency Village — bought by a collective of filmmakers and renamed, now programmed by American Cinematheque.
venues.name: Directors Village

venues.bio: An El Segundo single-screen theater showing classic films, with shows opening on its Mighty Wurlitzer theatre organ.
venues.name: Old Town Music Hall

venues.bio: UCLA's art museum in Westwood, where the UCLA Film & Television Archive screens its repertory film series.
venues.name: Hammer Museum

venues.bio: A Los Feliz nonprofit library and research center that hosts horror and cult film nights.
venues.name: Philosophical Research Society
